Why Plan Before You Build?

Every successful IT product starts with a plan. Jumping straight into building a website, app or database without a design document wastes time and leads to costly mistakes. Design tools help developers, designers and clients agree on what the finished product should look like and how it should work — before a single line of code is written.

The exam requires you to know four main types of design tool: flow charts, mind maps, visualisation diagrams and wireframes. For each one you must be able to describe its components, name software that creates it, and weigh up its advantages and disadvantages.

Key Fact

The four design tools are flow charts, mind maps, visualisation diagrams and wireframes. Each suits a different planning purpose — process logic, brainstorming, appearance, and page layout respectively.

Flow Charts

A flow chart maps out a process step by step. It uses internationally recognised symbols: ovals (start/end), rectangles (process steps), diamonds (decisions with yes/no branches) and parallelograms (input/output). Arrows show the direction of flow.

Flow charts are ideal when you need to show logic — for example, how a login system checks a username and password before granting access. Software such as Microsoft Visio, Lucidchart and even PowerPoint can create them, or they can be hand-sketched.

Advantages: clear visual representation of logic; easy for technical and non-technical stakeholders to follow; standard symbols mean the chart is understood internationally; helps identify missing steps or infinite loops before coding begins.

Disadvantages: can become very large and complex for multi-step systems; symbols must be used correctly or the diagram is misleading; updating a hand-drawn chart is time-consuming when the design changes.

Mind Maps

A mind map is a brainstorming tool. A central idea sits in the middle, with branches radiating outwards to related topics, and sub-branches adding more detail. The spec identifies three specific types used in IT design projects.

A library mind map organises a collection of resources or assets — for example, mapping all the images, audio clips and text files needed for a website. A tunnel timeline mind map sequences tasks over time, showing what must happen before the next stage can begin. A presentation mind map structures the content and flow of a presentation or report.

Mind maps can be drawn by hand or created using software such as MindMeister, Coggle or Microsoft Word’s SmartArt feature. They are quick to produce and easy to update as ideas evolve.

A visualisation diagram (sometimes called a mock-up) shows the intended appearance of an IT product. It includes colours, images, fonts and the general layout — it looks like the real thing but is not interactive. It is useful for getting client sign-off on aesthetics before development starts.

A wireframe is a skeletal layout of a single screen or web page. It uses simple boxes, placeholder text and labels to show where navigation menus, images, headings, forms and buttons will sit — but it deliberately avoids colour or imagery so the focus stays on structure and usability. Wireframes are often the first design step because they are quick to produce and cheap to revise.

Both can be created by hand or using specialist software. Tools widely used in schools and the workplace include Balsamiq (wireframes), Figma (visualisation diagrams) and PowerPoint or Google Slides (both).

Key Fact

A flow chart uses four standard shapes: ovals (start/end), rectangles (process), diamonds (decision) and parallelograms (input/output). Using these symbols correctly is essential — the examiner rewards labelled, accurate designs.

Sketches vs Software

Design tools can be created either by hand (sketching on paper) or using software. Each approach has its place. Hand sketches are fast, require no technology, and are ideal for early-stage brainstorming when ideas are still forming. They are also exactly what the exam’s 8-mark “create” question requires — students hand-draw their design solution.

Software-created designs look more professional, are easier to share with clients and team members, and are much simpler to edit when changes are needed. The trade-off is that software takes longer to learn and requires access to the correct application. In a professional project, hand sketches are typically used first and then refined digitally.

Assessing Suitability

Choosing the right design tool for a given context is a key exam skill. Ask yourself: does the project need to show a process or logic (flow chart), explore ideas or assets (mind map), communicate intended appearance (visualisation diagram) or plan page structure (wireframe)? A scenario question might describe a developer building a new booking system — a flow chart suits the booking logic, a wireframe suits the booking form layout, and a visualisation diagram suits the client sign-off on colours and branding.

How Users Communicate with Devices

Every time you tap a screen, speak a command, click a mouse button or press a key, you are using an interaction method — a way of sending instructions to a device. The exam requires you to know the five named interaction methods, their advantages and disadvantages, and which contexts each one suits. This topic is highlighted in examiner reports as one of the least well-answered despite the methods being listed directly in the specification. This lesson treats them as the central topic and builds in the vocabulary to justify each choice in a scenario.

The Five User Interaction Methods

Gesture input uses finger movements on a touchscreen — swiping, pinching, tapping, holding and rotating. It is fast and intuitive for experienced users, enables natural manipulation of content (zoom, rotate, pan), and requires no separate input device. Disadvantages: it requires a touchscreen, it can be inaccurate for users with motor impairments, and gestures that are not visible or labelled (such as a three-finger swipe) can be difficult to discover or learn.

Keyboard input is fast and accurate for text entry and commands. Touch-typists can enter text much faster than any voice or gesture method. Keyboards support shortcuts (copy, paste, undo) that speed up workflows significantly. Disadvantages: keyboards usually need a stable surface; they are unsuitable in hands-free contexts (cooking, surgery, driving) or when sterile conditions must be maintained (an operating theatre touchscreen is cleanable; a keyboard collects bacteria in the gaps between keys).

Mouse input offers high precision — a skilled user can click tiny interface elements accurately, making it ideal for complex desktop software such as graphic design tools or data analysis dashboards. Disadvantages: a mouse requires a flat surface, a desk and a trained hand. It is less suitable for portable or on-the-move devices and may be inconvenient where an interface is designed for direct touch.

Touch input uses finger contact with a touchscreen. It is direct and intuitive — tapping an icon feels like physically pressing a button. Touch is the dominant interaction method on smartphones and tablets. Disadvantages: it requires a clean surface and clean dry hands to register accurately; it can leave fingerprints on the screen; small interface elements are hard to tap precisely; and prolonged touch interaction on a vertical screen (such as a smartboard) causes arm fatigue.

Voice input allows hands-free control — ideal for contexts where the user cannot or should not look at or touch a screen. A driver asking a navigation system for directions, a chef asking a smart speaker for a timer, or a surgeon requesting data in an operating theatre all benefit from voice interaction. Disadvantages: voice input is unreliable in noisy environments (a busy restaurant, a factory floor), can raise privacy concerns (the device must always be listening for a wake word), and may not work well for users with accents, speech impairments or quiet voices.

Key Fact

The five user interaction methods are: gesture (touchscreen, natural but requires touch hardware), keyboard (fast text entry, unsuitable hands-free), mouse (precise, requires flat surface), touch (direct, intuitive, small targets imprecise), voice (hands-free, unreliable in noisy environments). Context determines which is most suitable — there is no single “best” method.

Exam questions give a context and ask you to select and justify an interaction method. Work through the constraints of the scenario. An ATM in a public space: touch is suitable (direct, single-purpose task, no keyboard needed for PIN if a numerical touchpad is used); voice is unsuitable (public setting, privacy risk, noisy environment). A kitchen smart speaker: voice is ideal (cook’s hands may be wet or covered in food, eyes focused on the cooking); touch or gesture are unsuitable for the same reason. A graphic design workstation: mouse is best (pixel-level precision needed for editing); touch is unsuitable (not accurate enough for fine manipulation). A hospital patient kiosk: touch is suitable (simple form-based interaction, no keyboard needed); gesture may be unsuitable if the patient has motor impairments — large buttons suit this context better.

The Internet of Everything (IoE) — Digital Interactivity

The Internet of Everything (IoE) connects not just computers and phones but everyday physical devices — smart bulbs, fitness trackers, industrial sensors, cars, fridges — to the internet and to each other. The spec requires you to know two types of IoE digital interactivity: device-to-device and human-to-device.

Device-to-device interactivity (also called machine-to-machine, or M2M) is communication between devices without human involvement. A fitness tracker automatically sends step count and heart rate data to a smartphone app. A smart thermostat detects that the house is empty using a linked door sensor and adjusts the heating automatically. A factory machine reports its performance data to a central monitoring system every few seconds. The human set up the system originally, but the ongoing data exchange is automatic.

Human-to-device interactivity in the IoE is when a person directly controls or communicates with a connected device. Asking a smart speaker to play music, unlocking a smart lock via a smartphone app, or adjusting the temperature on a smart thermostat using a voice command are all examples. The interaction uses the five methods covered earlier — voice, touch, gesture — but the device is part of the wider IoE network rather than a standalone computer.

The spec also requires you to know how digital devices in the IoE can be tailored to meet the needs of the end user. This links back to the accessibility demographics from Lesson 11. Examples: a smart TV can be configured to display larger subtitles for a hard-of-hearing user; a smart speaker can be set to respond more slowly and clearly for users with cognitive processing needs; a wearable medical monitor can alert a caregiver automatically when a reading goes outside a safe range (device-to-device), removing the need for the patient to remember to check a screen.

Tailoring might also mean physical adaptations: a large-button TV remote for users with reduced dexterity, voice-only control for users who cannot use their hands, or haptic feedback (vibration) for users who are visually impaired and cannot see on-screen confirmation of an action.

Key Fact

Device-to-device (M2M): automated data exchange between connected devices with no human involvement — e.g. fitness tracker syncing data to a phone app. Human-to-device: a person directly controls or communicates with a connected IoE device — e.g. using a smartphone app to unlock a smart lock.

What Does an Operating System Do?

Before you can design or use an HCI, something must manage the hardware, run the software and provide the interface layer between the user and the machine. That something is the operating system (OS). Every digital device — from a smartphone in your pocket to a server in a data centre — runs an operating system. The OS performs three core jobs: it manages hardware resources (telling the processor, RAM and storage when and how to be used), it runs software applications, and it presents the HCI through which users interact with the device.

This topic is flagged by examiners as content that is not covered in the coursework units — which means students who revise only from their NEA projects often miss it entirely. The exam asks you to name specific operating systems, describe their key characteristics and explain how the OS choice shapes the HCI design.

Desktop and Laptop Operating Systems

Windows is the dominant desktop OS in most business and educational environments. Its HCI is built around a taskbar at the bottom of the screen, a Start menu for launching applications and a windowed interface where multiple apps run simultaneously in resizable panels. Designers building for Windows can expect users to interact via mouse and keyboard, and to expect familiar navigation patterns such as right-click context menus.

Apple macOS runs exclusively on Apple’s own hardware. Its HCI uses a Dock at the bottom of the screen, a persistent menu bar at the top and a design language emphasised in Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines. macOS designers target a user base that expects visually polished, consistent interfaces with smooth animations. Software compatibility is narrower than Windows but the hardware and software ecosystem is tightly controlled.

Linux (and Ubuntu) is open-source and free. Ubuntu is a widely used distribution designed to be accessible to non-technical users. Linux HCIs vary significantly: some use graphical desktops resembling Windows; others are primarily command-line interfaces used by developers and system administrators. Because Linux can be configured so freely, HCI designers targeting Linux environments must account for a wide range of possible interface configurations.

Unix is the historical foundation from which macOS evolved (via Apple's acquisition of NeXT, which was BSD-based). Linux is a separately written, Unix-inspired operating system — it is Unix-compatible but was not derived from Unix source code. Today it is found mainly in enterprise-grade server environments and academic institutions. Unix systems are typically operated via command-line interfaces, so they are not usually the target environment for consumer-facing HCI design — but the exam requires you to know it exists and its primary use context.

Chrome OS is Google’s operating system for Chromebook devices, popular in schools. It supports web apps and, on compatible devices, Android and Linux applications. Designers should consider responsive web design, native-app patterns and offline use.

Key Fact

The eight operating systems named in the specification are: Windows (business/education desktops), Apple macOS (Apple hardware), Apple iOS (iPhone/iPad), Android (most smartphones and tablets), Chrome OS (Chromebook laptops), Ubuntu (user-friendly Linux distribution), Linux (servers, developers), Unix (enterprise servers, academic systems).

Mobile Operating Systems

Apple iOS has a tightly controlled app ecosystem. App Store apps must pass Apple’s review process, although some regions allow alternative distribution. HCI design for iOS follows Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines closely: consistent navigation patterns, specific button sizes and placement conventions, and design expectations around gestures (swipe up to go home, long press for options). The closed ecosystem means fewer device variants to design for, but developers must follow Apple’s rules.

Android is open-source and used on devices from many different manufacturers. This makes it the most widely used mobile OS globally. However, it creates a design challenge: Android runs on devices with hugely varying screen sizes, processor speeds and display resolutions. A designer targeting Android must test across multiple device types and plan for responsive layouts that adapt to different dimensions. The Google Play Store distributes Android apps, but the approval process is less restrictive than Apple’s.

The OS creates the environment in which an HCI must operate — and each OS brings its own conventions, constraints and user expectations. On Windows, users expect right-click menus, resizable windows and keyboard shortcuts. On iOS, users expect swipe gestures, a consistent bottom navigation bar and no right-click functionality. On Linux, power users may prefer a command-line interface for speed and control. On Chrome OS, the interface must work primarily within a browser window.

Designing against platform conventions can produce poor HCI. Navigation should use a pattern suited to the app and the available screen space. An interface that relies on hover effects will not work on any touch-based OS. Knowing the OS is therefore not optional in HCI design — it determines the interaction vocabulary the designer must use.

Digital Platforms

Operating systems run software — and the software environment the HCI is designed for is called the digital platform. The four digital platform types named in the specification are: database, mobile app, spreadsheet and website.

A database platform presents data in structured tables and forms. The HCI for a database typically includes search fields, data entry forms, filter controls and tabular displays. Users are often data professionals rather than general consumers. A mobile app is installed on a smartphone or tablet and uses the device’s touchscreen conventions. Its HCI must use large tap targets, limited navigation depth and mobile-specific interaction patterns. A spreadsheet platform (such as a desktop application or web-based tool) presents data in a grid of cells. HCI features include formula input, cell formatting and chart generation — designed for numeric analysis rather than casual browsing. A website runs in a browser and must be designed to work across different browsers, screen sizes and operating systems simultaneously. Responsive design — the ability to adapt the layout to different screen widths — is essential.

Exam questions on digital platforms often ask you to select and justify a platform for a scenario. Work through the user and task. A local GP surgery wanting to record patient appointment data with search and filter functionality → database (structured data, professional users). A national retailer wanting customers to browse and buy products on their phones → mobile app (touchscreen interaction, push notifications, stored payment details). A finance department needing to model budget forecasts → spreadsheet (formula-based calculations, chart output). A charity wanting to reach the widest possible audience with an information campaign → website (works on any device/OS without installation).

Key Fact

The four digital platforms are: database (structured data entry and retrieval, form-based HCI), mobile app (touchscreen interaction, large tap targets, installed on device), spreadsheet (grid-cell numerical data, formula input, charts), website (browser-based, responsive across devices and OS, no installation needed).

Why Hardware Shapes Interface Design

Every HCI — whether it is a banking app on a phone, a self-checkout screen at a supermarket, or a fitness tracker on your wrist — runs on real hardware. The hardware choices available to a designer directly affect what the interface can look, feel and do. In the exam, questions on this topic often ask you to select suitable hardware for a given scenario or explain the impact of a hardware constraint on interface design. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and reasoning to answer those questions confidently.

Display Type

The type of display screen shapes what an HCI can show and how users interact with it. The four main display types are LCD (Liquid Crystal Display), OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode), e-ink, and capacitive touchscreen.

LCD screens are cost-effective and widely used on laptops, desktop monitors and retail tills. They require a backlight, which makes them less energy-efficient than OLED but suitable when cost matters. OLED screens produce richer colours and deeper blacks because each pixel lights itself. This makes them ideal for premium smartphone and TV interfaces where visual quality drives the user experience. E-ink screens use almost no power and are easy to read in bright sunlight — making them ideal for e-readers and bus-stop information displays that need long battery life and outdoor readability. Capacitive touchscreens allow finger-based interaction and are embedded in smartphones, self-service kiosks and point-of-sale terminals. The interface design must account for this: buttons need to be large enough to tap accurately, and hover states used on desktop menus become irrelevant.

Display Size

Screen size directly determines how much information can fit on the display at once and how the interface is laid out. A smartwatch screen (typically 1–2 inches) can display only a few lines of text or a single metric at a time — its HCI must use large icons, simple swipe gestures and minimal text. A smartphone screen (typically 5–7 inches) supports richer layouts but designers still favour mobile-first principles: large tap targets, scrollable content and simplified navigation. A laptop or desktop screen (13–34 inches) allows multi-column layouts, dense menus and complex dashboards that would be unreadable on smaller screens. A smartboard (interactive whiteboard, 55–86 inches) is designed for group use from a distance — text must be large enough to read across a classroom, and the interface should support large gestures rather than precise taps.

Key Fact

Display type and size together shape the entire HCI layout. A small OLED touchscreen (smartwatch) forces minimal-text, icon-based design; a large non-touch LCD monitor allows dense multi-column layouts. Matching display choice to context is a core design decision.

Memory (RAM) vs Storage — A Critical Distinction

This distinction is explicitly flagged in examiner reports as a source of lost marks. Many students confuse memory and storage, or use the two words interchangeably. They are different.

RAM (Random Access Memory) is temporary. It holds whatever the processor is actively working with at this moment — the running app, the open browser tabs, the data being processed. When you switch the device off, RAM is wiped completely. More RAM means the device can keep more things open and running simultaneously without slowing down. For HCI design, insufficient RAM means sluggish animations, delayed responses when typing, and apps crashing when multitasking. A banking app with smooth transitions and real-time balance updates needs sufficient RAM to function as designed.

Storage (on a hard drive, SSD or flash memory) is permanent. It holds files, apps and the operating system even when the device is switched off. More storage means more apps and files can be saved on the device. For HCI design, storage capacity affects how many features an app can install locally versus requiring an internet connection to stream. It does not affect the speed of the running interface directly — that is RAM’s role.

The examiner report is explicit: many students write about “memory” when they mean storage, and vice versa. A question such as “Explain how RAM affects the performance of an HCI” requires you to say that RAM is temporary working memory for actively running processes, and that insufficient RAM causes slowdowns and crashes during use. Saying “more memory means more files can be saved” scores zero — that describes storage, not RAM.

Use this quick test: if data disappears when you turn the device off, it is RAM. If data is still there after switching off and on, it is storage. The exam will give you a scenario (e.g. a self-service kiosk) and ask you to explain the impact of RAM or storage — apply this distinction directly to the scenario.

Key Fact

RAM is temporary working memory — it holds actively running data and is wiped on shutdown. Storage is permanent — it holds files and apps between sessions. RAM affects interface speed and responsiveness; storage affects how much can be saved locally on the device.

Processing Power

The processor (CPU) executes the instructions that make an HCI function. Processing power determines how quickly the device can carry out calculations, render graphics and respond to user input. An interface that runs on a low-powered processor — such as an embedded system in a washing machine — must be simple and lightweight: minimal graphics, no animations, limited options. A high-powered desktop processor can run complex data dashboards with real-time charts, animated transitions and multiple simultaneous background processes.

When a question gives you a scenario — “a hospital reception kiosk” or “a portable stock-checking device for a warehouse” — work through each hardware consideration in turn. For display: what screen size does the context require? Does the user interact by touch or indirectly? For RAM: does the HCI need to keep multiple processes running at once, or is it a single-purpose tool? For storage: does it need to store data locally, or does it connect to a network database? For processing power: does the interface need real-time updates, animations or heavy calculations?

A hospital reception kiosk might need a large capacitive touchscreen (accessible to users of varying abilities), moderate RAM (running a booking system and checking in patients simultaneously) and modest local storage (it connects to the hospital’s main server rather than storing records locally). A wearable fitness tracker needs a small OLED touchscreen, minimal RAM (it only tracks one or two metrics) and very low processing power — because everything must fit within a tiny battery budget.
